kurz: Why return patterns shrink after publication and how to check whether they ever existed at all.

bloecke.md:
An [[anomaly]] is a return pattern that an accepted pricing model does not explain. Securities with a particular characteristic systematically earn returns that differ from what their measured risk would suggest. Since the 1970s, financial research has published several hundred such patterns. What happened to them after publication is more revealing than the findings themselves.

Three explanations are possible for the decline in measured premiums. First, the pattern may never have existed and may merely have been an artefact of data selection. Second, it may have existed and been eliminated after publication by investors trading on it. Third, it may persist because it compensates for a risk or an inconvenience that many investors do not want to bear. In hindsight, all three cases look the same, because in each of them the measured premium shrinks. They differ only in what you can expect for the future.

## Calendar effects

In 1976, Rozeff and Kinney documented strikingly high January returns for an equal-weighted US index. In 1983, Keim showed that the effect was mainly attributable to small companies and that about half of it fell in the first trading week of the year. The usual explanation was tax-motivated selling in December, with the securities being bought back in January. In 1980, French described the weekend effect. According to his findings, the average Monday return on the US market from 1953 to 1977 was negative.

Both effects were widely published, and both are barely measurable in later data for liquid blue chips. In his 2003 survey of anomalies and market efficiency, Schwert concluded that the size effect, the weekend effect and related patterns weakened or disappeared after the publication of the respective paper.

For German securities accounts, there is the additional point that taxation is regulated differently. Under Section 43a(3) EStG (Income Tax Act), the custodian bank keeps running loss offset pots (Verlustverrechnungstöpfe). Under Section 20(6) EStG, losses from sales of shares can only be offset against gains on shares, and unused losses are carried forward to the following year without time limit. To offset losses against gains of the same year, you do have to sell by the end of December here too. Unlike in the US, however, there is no wash-sale rule that disallows the loss for tax purposes if the same securities are bought back within 30 days of the sale. Sale and repurchase can therefore take place on the same day, and there is no need to buy back in January. The explanation based on the US tax calendar can therefore only be applied to a German securities account to a limited extent.

The following illustrative calculation assumes that the Monday effect is stable and amounts to 0.10 percentage points a week. Over 52 weeks, this works out at around 5.3% a year.

To exploit the effect, you have to get in and out 52 times. Each round trip costs the full bid-ask spread. At 0.05% per side, this gives 52 × 0.10% = 5.2% in trading costs even before order fees, taxes and market impact, so that nothing is left net.

In general, an effect is only as large as the gap between the signal and trading costs. That is why the strongest documented anomalies have historically been found where trading is most expensive, namely in very small, illiquid stocks.

## Cross-sectional effects

The three best-known characteristic-based effects have lasted considerably longer than the calendar patterns, but they too have become smaller since their publication. Banz described the excess return of small companies in 1981, Fama and French the value effect in 1992, and Jegadeesh and Titman momentum in 1993. The following table compares the long-short premiums from the Kenneth French Data Library before and after the respective publication date.

bloecke.md:
The three factors have developed very differently. Momentum has lost the most in absolute terms and has been close to zero since 2000. Value has also shrunk considerably but has kept a positive premium. Size disappeared after publication, and even calculated over a hundred years, SMB is not statistically significant, with t = 1.82.

For your portfolio, this means that a small-cap ETF contains small caps, but on this evidence it does not establish any claim to a premium. Diversification can still be a reason to buy one, but it does not come with any promise of a higher return.

## The McLean and Pontiff study

The cleanest measurement of the effect comes from McLean and Pontiff (Journal of Finance 2016). They examined 97 published return predictors and reconstructed three returns for each: in the original sample, in the period after the original sample but before publication, and after publication.

Out of sample, but still before publication, the return was on average 26% below the original finding. This discount is due to overfitting. The authors of the original studies, consciously or unconsciously, chose the period, filters and definition of the characteristic so that the result looked good in their own sample. After publication, the return was 58% below the original finding. The additional 32 percentage points are due to arbitrage, as investors learn about the pattern and partly eliminate it through their trading. After publication, returns remained higher where the stocks were illiquid and carried high idiosyncratic risk, that is, where arbitrage is most expensive. For liquid stocks with low idiosyncratic risk, they were lower.

bloecke.unter: Average across 97 predictors according to McLean/Pontiff (2016), normalised to the original finding = 100. The first step shows overfitting, the second the learning of investors.

bloecke.md:
## Data mining and p-hacking

The 42% that remains on average is an average across patterns that made it into a good academic journal. It says nothing about how many patterns were tested in total, and therein lies the problem.

A significance test at the 5% level by definition allows a false alarm in one case out of twenty. Researchers who test a hundred signals and publish only the one that clears the hurdle are thus certain to get a publication, but gain no robust knowledge. The problem is made worse by degrees of freedom that can each be justified individually: start year, exclusion of financial stocks, equal weighting instead of value weighting, treatment of outliers or a different definition of a metric. Each of these variants is a hidden test. This practice is called [[p-hacking]], and the discarded variants do not appear in any statistics.

bloecke.formel: Expected chance hits = Number of tests × Significance level
bloecke.erklaerung: The number of spurious findings grows linearly with the number of signals tested. This includes the signals that were never published.
variablen: all signals and evaluation variants tested, not only the published ones
usual threshold 5%, corresponding to about t = 1.96
bloecke.beispiel: 447 × 0.05 = 22. Even if none of these 447 patterns were genuine, around 22 would be expected to clear the usual hurdle by chance alone. Conversely, with 300 simultaneous tests and an overall error probability of 5%, each individual test needs a level of 0.05 / 300 = 0.000167. This corresponds to a t-statistic of around 3.8.

bloecke.md: Hou, Xue and Zhang recalculated 447 published anomalies using a uniform methodology, that is, with value weighting instead of equal weighting and without overweighting microcaps. Of these, 64% failed the usual hurdle of t = 1.96, and 85% failed at t = 3.0. The main reason was the construction of the original studies, not fraud. Many original findings were based on very small stocks. These microcaps make up around 60% of all US shares but only about 3% of market capitalisation. With equal weighting, they therefore make up the bulk of the portfolio, but in reality they cannot be traded in any meaningful size.

bloecke.unter: According to Hou/Xue/Zhang. The bottom bar shows how many hits would be expected from 447 tests by chance alone; the 161 confirmed anomalies are well above this, but far below 447.
kategorien: published and significant in the original

bloecke.md:
## Harvey's critique and the opposing view

Campbell Harvey drew the most far-reaching conclusion from this. Together with Liu and Zhu, he argued in 2016 in the Review of Financial Studies that the large number of factors tested simultaneously makes the usual significance threshold worthless. A new factor, they argued, must reach t = 3.0 instead of 1.96. In his presidential address to the American Finance Association, he described a considerable part of the published findings in financial economics as probably false. John Cochrane had already spoken earlier of a “zoo” of new factors.

The opposing view is also well founded. Using a hierarchical Bayesian method, Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen reach the opposite conclusion. According to their analysis, the majority of factors can be replicated, cluster into around 13 themes and hold out of sample in 93 countries. Baltussen, Swinkels and van Vliet examined 24 global premiums from 1800 to 2016 in equities, bonds, commodities and currencies and found the great majority confirmed. The dispute is therefore less about whether the premiums exist than about how large they will be in future.

The estimates for this are low. Chen and Velikov worked through 204 long-short anomalies, taking into account spreads, the publication effect and modern trading technology. They arrived at an average of 4 basis points a month, around 0.5% a year, and at about 10 basis points for the best anomalies, just over 1.2% a year. Market impact, product fees and taxes have not yet been deducted from these figures.

Huang, Song and Xiang measured how smart beta indices performed before and after the launch of the associated ETF. In the back-calculated period beforehand, they achieved an excess return of around 3% a year, and afterwards minus 0.5% to minus 1% a year. According to their analysis, the cause lies in optimising the index rules to fit the past. According to their results, a capacity limit does not explain the decline.

Legally, this is only partly covered. Under Section 63(6) WpHG (Securities Trading Act), information from investment services firms must be fair, clear and not misleading. Article 44 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 requires simulated past performance to be based on actual data for substantially similar instruments or indices and not to be the most prominent element of the presentation. The PRIIPs key information document under Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 shows scenarios that are also derived from historical data. The back-calculation on an index provider's factsheet, on the other hand, is often not covered by these requirements at all. Yet it is precisely this back-calculation that is quoted in marketing.

schritte.text: A single t-value is worthless without the number of variants tested. For a provider with dozens of indices, a fair hurdle is closer to 3 to 4 than to 1.96.
The pattern should be confirmed in another country, another asset class or another period, ideally in a period the author did not know when designing it.

Check whether the calculation was equal-weighted or value-weighted, whether microcaps are included and whether the portfolio is long-short or long-only. A long-only product retains only a fraction of the academic factor exposure.
Turnover, spread, TER and market impact must be taken into account. With a gross premium of 1% to 2%, costs decide whether the net result is a plus or a minus.
Possible explanations are risk, behavioural patterns or institutional constraints. A pattern without an explanation outside the data is just a correlation that has yet to prove itself.

bloecke.md:
The term “half-life” suggests a steady decay in which half disappears every X years. Anomalies do not behave like that. The decline happens in jumps and is triggered by an event, such as publication, the launch of a product or inclusion in standard software. This is followed by a long phase of heavy statistical noise in which the data can hardly show whether a residual premium exists.

The dispersion across rolling ten-year windows since 1926 shows how strong the noise is. HML was negative in 14% of these windows, momentum in 21% and SMB in 35%. Even over twenty years, SMB remains negative in 19.5% of the windows. The statement “the factor is dead” after the value low of 2020 was therefore just as premature as the claim that the factor had returned after 2021 and 2022. An investor's lifetime is too short to be able to rely statistically on a premium.

A return pattern is initially just a statement about a particular sample. For a newly promoted pattern, a realistic expectation is well below the backtest. First deduct the discount for overfitting, then the one for investor learning and finally the costs. What remains after that is rarely enough to justify deviating from the broad market portfolio.

mitnehmen: Calendar effects such as the January and Monday effects have practically disappeared in liquid markets since their publication and were below trading costs anyway.
For 97 predictors, McLean/Pontiff measure a decline of 26% out of sample and of 58% after publication, leaving around 42% of the original finding.
Of 447 recalculated anomalies, only 36% clear the hurdle t > 1.96 under a uniform methodology, and 15% the hurdle t > 3.0.
With hundreds of signals tested simultaneously, t = 2 is no proof; Harvey/Liu/Zhu require more than 3.0, and a strict Bonferroni correction would be higher still.
The size effect has been negative since 1981, value and momentum have shrunk but not disappeared, and the realistic residual premium after costs is in the range of 0 to 2 percentage points.

begriffe.text: A return pattern that an accepted pricing model does not explain. One example is a systematic excess return on shares with a particular characteristic that cannot be explained by their market risk.
Searching data sets for patterns without a prior hypothesis. In capital market research, it leads to chance findings being published as regularities, because only the successful tests are visible.
Consciously or unconsciously varying the period, filters, weighting and definition of metrics until a result clears the significance threshold. Each discarded variant is a hidden additional test.

Problem that arises when many hypotheses are tested simultaneously. The number of false alarms then rises linearly with the number of tests, and the usual significance threshold of t = 1.96 loses its meaning.
Testing a discovered pattern on data that were not used in its construction, for example from other periods, countries or asset classes. It is the most important safeguard against overfitting.

The decline in an anomaly's return after its publication, because investors know the pattern and trade on it. McLean/Pontiff put it at around 32 percentage points in addition to the overfitting discount.
